a: Markgraf took part in the uneventful advance toward Sunderland between 18 and 20 October. From 21 October to 2 November, the ship conducted unit training with III Squadron, and two days afterward she formally rejoined that squadron. On the 5th, a pair of U-boats ran aground on the Danish coast; light forces were dispatched to recover them, and III Squadron, then in the North Sea on its way to Wilhelmshaven, received orders to provide cover. In the course of this operation, the British submarine J1 torpedoed both Grosser Kurfürst and Kronprinz, inflicting moderate damage. Throughout most of 1917, Markgraf was engaged in guard duty in the North Sea, broken only by a refit in January and occasional unit training in the Baltic.
h: Markgraf was present for the uneventful advance in the direction of Sunderland on 18 – 20 October . Unit training with the III Squadron followed from 21 October to 2 November . Two days later , the ship formally rejoined III Squadron . On the 5th , a pair of U @-@ boats grounded on the Danish coast . Light forces were sent to recover the vessels , and III Squadron , which was in the North Sea en route to Wilhelmshaven , was ordered to cover them . During the operation , the British submarine J1 torpedoed both Grosser Kurfürst and Kronprinz and caused moderate damage . For most of 1917 , Markgraf was occupied with guard duties in the North Sea , interrupted only by a refit period in January and periodic unit training in the Baltic .

a: Innis's writings on communication examine how media shape the culture and development of civilizations. He argued, for instance, that a balance between oral and written forms of communication helped Greek civilization flourish in the 5th century BC. At the same time, he cautioned that Western civilization is now endangered by powerful, advertising-driven media preoccupied with "present-mindedness" and the "continuous, systematic, ruthless destruction of elements of permanence essential to cultural activity." His intellectual partnership with Eric A. Havelock laid the foundations of the "Toronto School of Communication," which went on to inspire later members of the school, namely Marshall McLuhan and Edmund Snow Carpenter.
h: Innis 's writings on communication explore the role of media in shaping the culture and development of civilizations . He warned , however , that Western civilization is now imperiled by powerful , advertising @-@ driven media obsessed by " present @-@ mindedness " and the " continuous , systematic , ruthless destruction of elements of permanence essential to cultural activity " . His intellectual bond with Eric A. Havelock formed the foundations of the “ Toronto School of Communication ” which provided a source of inspiration for future members of the school : Marshall McLuhan and Edmund Snow Carpenter .

a: Beginning his first full season as York's manager, Nigel Worthington completed eight permanent signings over the summer. As the year turned, York sat only above the relegation zone on goal difference, but a 17-match unbeaten run then carried the team to seventh place in the 24-team 2013-14 Football League Two. That finish earned York a place in the play-offs, where they were knocked out in the semi-final by Fleetwood Town. In the 2013-14 FA Cup, Football League Cup, and Football League Trophy, York were each eliminated in their opening match.

a: The development of special forces within the Romanian Land Forces culminated in the creation of the 1st Special Operations Regiment on 1 August 2009, with its headquarters at Târgu Mureş. The unit was subsequently reorganized as the 6th Special Operations Brigade on 25 October 2011, comprising a special operations battalion, two paratrooper battalions, and a logistic battalion.
h: The evolution of the special forces within the Romanian Land Forces led to the establishment of the 1st Special Operations Regiment on 1 August 2009 , headquartered at Târgu Mureş . a: The ship was loaned to the Royal Hellenic Navy on 10 February and recommissioned by them on 25 March under the name Salamis. She sustained damage while working up at Scapa Flow and underwent repairs at Hull from 28 April to 13 June. Salamis was then assigned to escort duty at Gibraltar until October, when she was transferred to the Aegean and served with the 12th (Greek) Destroyer Flotilla for the remainder of the war. Following the war she served as a training ship until she was returned to the Royal Navy at Malta on 9 October 1951. On 15 April 1952 she arrived at Rosyth under tow to be broken up by Metal Industries, Limited.

With their ammunition spent and their position surrounded, they were compelled to surrender.

a: The conclave opened on 15 February 1769, with only 27 cardinals taking part at first. Exploiting both the small electorate and the absence of the French and Spanish cardinals, the Zelanti sought to bring about a swift election of Cardinal Flavio Chigi. In one ballot he fell just two votes short of the required majority. The Zelanti's efforts drew strong protests from the ambassadors of France and Spain, but to their advantage, Cardinal Orsini, protector of the Kingdom of Naples and the only crown-cardinal present in the early ballots, managed to enlist several neutral cardinals to block Chigi's candidacy.
h: The conclave began on February 15 , 1769 . Initially only 27 cardinals participated . Zelanti , taking advantage of the small number of the electors and the absence of the French and Spanish cardinals , tried to achieve a quick election of Cardinal Flavio Chigi . In one ballot he was only two votes short of being elected . The efforts of Zelanti met with strong protests from the ambassadors of France and Spain , but , fortunately for them , Cardinal Orsini , protector of the Kingdom of Naples and the only crown @-@ cardinal present in the early ballots , was able to join some neutral cardinals to block Chigi ’ s candidature .

a: The German chemist Andreas Libavius was familiar with metallic antimony in 1615, having produced it by adding iron to a molten mixture of antimony sulfide, salt, and potassium tartrate. This method yielded antimony with a crystalline or starred surface.
h: The metal antimony was known to German chemist Andreas Libavius in 1615 who obtained it by adding iron to a molten mixture of antimony sulfide , salt and potassium tartrate . This procedure produced antimony with a crystalline or starred surface .

a: Antimony(III) sulfide is used in the heads of certain safety matches. Antimony-124 is paired with beryllium in neutron sources, where the gamma rays it emits trigger the photodisintegration of beryllium; the resulting neutrons carry an average energy of 24 keV. Antimony sulfides have also been found to help stabilize the friction coefficient in automotive brake pad materials.

a: The Patriarchal Cathedral was destroyed after the Ottomans took the Bulgarian capital following their Siege of Tarnovo on 17 July 1393. It was completely rebuilt in the 20th century by a team led by the architect Boyan Kuzupov, whose work ran from 1978 to 1981 and was timed to coincide with Bulgaria's 1300th anniversary. Even so, the church did not reopen to visitors until November 1985, once the contemporary murals had been completed. Its ruins have been protected as a national antiquity since 1927, and in 1967 they were declared an architectural monument of culture of national importance. As part of the Tsarevets architectural reserve, the church is also counted among the 100 Tourist Sites of Bulgaria.
h: The Patriarchal Cathedral was destroyed after the Ottomans captured the Bulgarian capital after their Siege of Tarnovo on 17 July 1393 . The church was fully reconstructed in the 20th century ; reconstruction works were carried out by a team under architect Boyan Kuzupov . These commenced in 1978 and were finished in 1981 , to mark Bulgaria 's 1300th anniversary . However , it was not until November 1985 , when the contemporary murals were finished , that the church was opened once again for visitors . The church 's ruins have been protected as a national antiquity since 1927 ; in 1967 , they were proclaimed an architectural monument of culture of national importance . As part of the Tsarevets architectural reserve , it is also listed among the 100 Tourist Sites of Bulgaria .

a: Built atop a late Roman church and reconstructed during the 1970s and 1980s, the cathedral follows a cross-domed plan, with a bell tower and a triple apse. Lavishly ornamented both inside and out, its interior walls now display modern frescoes, and it is because of these frescoes that the building has not been reconsecrated. Although it no longer functions as a Christian place of worship, it has been open to visitors since 1985.
h: Standing on top of a late Roman church , the cathedral , reconstructed in the 1970s and 1980s , follows a cross @-@ domed plan with a bell tower and a triple apse . a: In January 1099, as the company of Raymond IV of Toulouse made its way to Jerusalem during the First Crusade, it was attacked by the garrison of Hisn al-Akrad, the predecessor of the Krak, who harassed Raymond's foragers. The next day Raymond advanced on the castle and found it abandoned. The crusaders occupied it briefly in February of that year but left it behind as they resumed their march toward Jerusalem. Lasting occupation did not begin until 1110, when Tancred, Prince of Galilee, seized the site. This early castle differed considerably from the surviving structure, and none of it remains at the location today.
h: In January 1099 on the journey to Jerusalem during the First Crusade , the company of Raymond IV of Toulouse came under attack from the garrison of Hisn al @-@ Akrad , the forerunner of the Krak , who harried Raymond 's foragers . a: Geologists have long debated why the slide debris traveled as far as it did. One early hypothesis, the "air cushion" theory, held that a layer of air became trapped between the rock mass and the mountain, allowing the rock to travel farther than would otherwise be expected. A competing theory, "acoustic fluidization," proposes that large masses of material generate seismic energy that lowers friction and lets the debris flow down the mountain as if it were a fluid. To describe the Frank Slide, geologists coined the term "debris avalanche."
h: Geologists have debated about what caused the slide debris to travel the distance it did . The " air cushion " theory , an early hypothesis , postulated that a layer of air was trapped between the mass of rock and the mountain , which caused the rock to move a greater distance than would otherwise be expected . " Acoustic fluidization " is another theory , which suggests that large masses of material create seismic energy that reduces friction and causes the debris to flow down the mountain as though it is a fluid . Geologists created the term " debris avalanche " to describe the Frank Slide .

a: Galveston contains six historic districts, with more than 60 structures of architectural significance listed in the National Register of Historic Places. The Silk Stocking National Historic District, situated between Broadway and Seawall Boulevard and bounded by Ave. K, 23rd St., Ave. P, and 26th St., holds a collection of historic homes built from the Civil War era through World War II. The East End Historic District, which lies on both sides of Broadway and Market Streets, comprises 463 buildings. The remaining historic districts are Cedar Lawn, Denver Court, and Fort Travis.

a: Off the coast of the United States, an extensive network of buoys is maintained by the National Data Buoy Center, with the United States Coast Guard handling their deployment and upkeep. In South Africa, the South African Weather Service deploys and recovers its own buoys, while the Meteorological Service of New Zealand carries out the same role for that country. Environment Canada operates and deploys buoys on behalf of Canada, and the Met Office in Great Britain places drifting buoys throughout both the northern and southern Atlantic oceans.
